data.reason: The KPI literally asks to deliver as many orders as possible within the promised times, so on_time_deliveries is the faithful primary goal. The KPI also allows revising the promised times and requires that customer-worsening changes be justified by their measured effect on customers. Option 1 meets that requirement by monitoring SLA-independent measures (p95_wait_s, unfinished) alongside late_deliveries. Option 2 would guard against gaming but would reject rule changes the KPI wants, those that raise the on-time count at a small cost in tail wait. The gaming risk is better handled by the rule that every SLA change is decided by a human after customer impact (p95_wait_s, max_wait_s, unfinished) has been reported. No measurements exist yet (period 1), so no table values are cited. No numeric targets or guards are set because the KPI states none. I follow the LLM's recommendation.
assumptions: Order volume is the same across runs with the same seed and demand, so on_time_deliveries and on_time_rate rank options the same way.
p95_wait_s and unfinished are measured independently of the SLA thresholds.
Any DELIVERY_SLA proposal will report p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished before a human decides.
unknowns: Baseline values of on_time_deliveries, p95_wait_s, unfinished and late_deliveries under the current rules.
Whether the operator would accept some rise in customer wait in exchange for more on-time deliveries, and how much.
Whether company-level effects will lead to rule changes being rejected in voting even when they improve the town total.

follow_ups.text: When the first DELIVERY_SLA change is proposed, decide whether its measured effect on customers (p95_wait_s, max_wait_s, unfinished) justifies it, and whether to set an explicit limit on acceptable customer wait.
